pages.name: The top of a curve
pages.task: The curve y = 6x − x² has slope 6 − 2x. At what x is its top?
pages.why: 6 − 2x = 0 gives x = 3. The height there is 18 − 9 = 9. You find the top of an efficiency curve the same way.

pages.name: Two branches
pages.text: A real transformer is the ideal one plus two branches. The shunt branch sits across the supply and stands for the core. The series branch sits in line with the load and stands for the windings. Only the series branch's current changes with the load.

pages.name: Iron stays put
pages.text: The copper loss grows with the square of the load. It is 400 W at full load and 100 W at half. The iron loss stays at 100 W, because the supply holds the flux at 1.88 mWb.

pages.text: At full load and unity power factor, 10,000 W comes out and 500 W is lost. That is 95.2%. At 0.8 power factor, only 8000 W comes out for the same losses. That is 94.1%.

pages.task: The same transformer runs at half load, unity power factor. What is its efficiency?
pages.why: Copper loss = 400 × 0.25 = 100 W. So the losses are 200 W in all. 5000 ÷ 5200 = 96.2%. That beats the 95.2% at full load.

pages.name: Another transformer
pages.task: A transformer has 64 W of iron loss and 400 W of full-load copper loss. At what load is it most efficient?
pages.why: 64 ÷ 400 = 0.16, and √0.16 = 0.4. So the peak is at 40%. Check: 400 × 0.4² = 64 W of copper loss, equal to the iron loss.

pages.name: A big unit, a light load
pages.task: A 100 kVA transformer tests at 500 W open circuit and 2000 W short circuit. It feeds a steady 20 kVA at unity power factor. What is its efficiency?
pages.why: Copper loss = 2000 × 0.2² = 80 W. So 500 W of the 580 W lost is iron loss. 20,000 ÷ 20,580 = 97.2%. At its 50% peak it would give 98.0%. A big transformer on a light load wastes mostly iron loss.
